title: Building a national digital ID: lessons from Nigeria's NIN
sum: Nigeria is moving from registering people to running a national trust layer. Its path, from enrollment at scale to authentication services and a new legal mandate, offers lessons for any country building digital identity.
body: In brief. Nigeria's National Identification Number (NIN) underpins banking, telecoms and government services. The World Bank-supported ID4D program is modernizing the identity core, NIMC launched the NINAuth authentication service in 2025, and the NIMC Act 2026 positions NIMC as the root authority for national digital identity.
Five lessons

1Coverage first

Enrollment at scale creates the base every other service depends on.

2Authentication, not just verification

Services need consented, real-time authentication rather than data lookups.

3Law and governance

A clear legal mandate defines who issues, who relies and who supervises.

4Trust services

PKI, signatures and wallets turn identity into a transaction layer.

5Ecosystem

Banks, telecoms and agencies must be able to integrate cheaply.

title: FAPI 2.0 as an open-banking security baseline: lessons from Singapore
sum: FAPI 2.0 turns OAuth into a profile fit for money and identity data. Singapore's national identity platform has set a deadline for it, offering a practical benchmark for banks and governments elsewhere.
body: In brief. The FAPI 2.0 Security Profile from the OpenID Foundation hardens OAuth 2.0 for high-value APIs. Singpass has set 31 December 2026 as the deadline for FAPI 2.0 integrations, making it one of the clearest national benchmarks.
What FAPI 2.0 adds

Pushed authorization requests

Request parameters go to the server directly, so they cannot be tampered with in the browser.

PKCE

Stops stolen authorization codes from being used.

Sender-constrained tokens

Tokens bound to the client with mTLS or DPoP are useless if stolen.

Strong client authentication

Private key JWT or mTLS instead of shared secrets.
Lessons for other markets

Set a date

A firm deadline moves an ecosystem faster than guidance.

Provide test tools

Conformance testing lowers the cost for relying parties.

Start with identity

Identity and consent APIs are the natural first target.

title: Real-time fraud decisioning: rules, machine learning and explanations regulators accept

Monitoring

title: Mule accounts: using graph analytics to stop them before funds move
sum: Every scam needs somewhere to send the money. Mule accounts look normal one by one; the pattern only appears when you look at the network of accounts, devices and payments around them.
body: In brief. Instant payments leave little time to recover stolen funds. Detecting the receiving mule account, ideally before it receives its first fraudulent transfer, is often more effective than chasing the money afterward.
What a mule network looks like

Shared devices

Several accounts opened or used from the same phones.

Fan-in, fan-out

Many small inbound transfers followed by fast outbound transfers.

Recycled details

Reused contact details, addresses or onboarding patterns.

Short life

Accounts dormant after opening, then suddenly very active.
How graph analytics helps

1Build the graph

Link accounts, customers, devices, IPs and counterparties.

2Score communities

Find clusters that behave like known mule rings.

3Act early

Hold, review or restrict accounts before funds arrive.

4Learn

Feed confirmed cases back to models and share where the law allows.
Governance matters
Graph models influence decisions about real customers. They need explainable outputs, human review for adverse actions and data-protection controls over what is linked and for how long.

title: RASP false positives: protecting apps without blocking real customers
sum: Runtime protection that blocks too much becomes the support desk's biggest problem. The goal is not maximum blocking. It is the right response to each signal, tuned on real devices.
body: In brief. Runtime application self-protection (RASP) detects rooting, hooking, emulators, debuggers and tampering. On a diverse device base, some of those signals fire on legitimate phones: custom ROMs, accessibility tools, developer settings or vendor quirks. Treating every signal as a block turns security into lost customers.
Graduated responses

Observe

Log the signal and feed it to the risk engine.

Restrict

Allow viewing but limit payments or new payees.

Step up

Ask for stronger authentication for the action.

Block

Reserve for clear tampering or regulatory requirements.
How to tune

1Measure by device model

Find signals that fire on specific brands or OS builds.

2Combine signals

Decide on combinations, not single flags.

3Update quickly

Ship detection updates without waiting for app releases where possible.

4Respect platform policy

Follow Google Play rules on app visibility and Accessibility.

title: Identity proofing to ETSI TS 119 461: what auditors actually check
sum: ETSI TS 119 461 sets the requirements for identity proofing behind qualified certificates and other trust services. Auditors look beyond the liveness vendor's brochure, at policies, evidence, threats and processes.
body: In brief. TS 119 461 defines how a trust service component proves who an applicant is, with a baseline level and an extended level for qualified certificates. Version 2 strengthened expectations around injection attacks and deepfakes.
What the auditor asks for

Policy and practice

A proofing policy and practice statement that match what the system actually does.

Use cases

Which proofing methods are allowed for which use cases, and why.

Evidence

What is collected, how it is protected, and how long it is kept.

Threat coverage

How presentation, injection and document fraud are addressed and tested.

Human review

When cases are escalated and how operators are trained.

Supplier control

How biometric and document vendors are assessed and monitored.
Typical gaps

Vendor test reports used as proof

A lab report on the biometric engine does not cover your full process.

Evidence scattered across systems

Auditors need a complete, linked record per applicant.

Recovery forgotten

Re-proofing after device loss must meet the same rules.

title: Zero Trust for public-service portals: where to start in the first six months
sum: Citizen portals connect millions of users to dozens of back-office systems. Zero Trust replaces broad network trust with a decision on every request. The first six months should focus on identity, the most exposed services and visibility.

sources.name: CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2.0

body: In brief. Zero Trust, as described in NIST SP 800-207, means no user, device or network location is trusted by default. Every access request is evaluated by a policy decision point and enforced close to the resource.
A six-month starting plan

1Month 1-2: identity

Strong authentication for staff and administrators; national eID for citizens.

2Month 2-3: protect the crown jewels

Put the most exposed services behind identity-aware gateways.

3Month 3-4: segment

Separate citizen, staff, partner and admin zones.

4Month 5-6: see and respond

Central logging, SOC use cases and automated response.
Common pitfalls

Buying a product, not an architecture

Zero Trust is a control model across identity, devices, networks, applications and data.

Forgetting service accounts

APIs and integrations need identities and policies too.

No measurement

title: Quantum-safe gateways for data centers: hybrid key exchange in practice
sum: Links between data centers, branches and partners carry data that attackers can record now and decrypt later. A quantum-safe gateway adds hybrid post-quantum key exchange without rewriting the applications behind it.

sources.name: IETF RFC 9370 - Multiple key exchanges in IKEv2

body: In brief. Hybrid key exchange combines a classical algorithm with ML-KEM, so a link stays secure as long as either one holds. Gateways can apply it at the network edge today, protecting long-lived data in transit while applications are migrated over time.
Where to start

Data center interconnects

Replication and backup traffic with long confidentiality needs.

Branch and partner links

Payment, card and interbank connections.

Administrative access

Privileged sessions to HSMs, CAs and core systems.
Design checklist

1Hybrid by default

Classical plus ML-KEM key exchange, per IETF hybrid approaches such as RFC 9370 for IKEv2.

2Strong identity

Device and user identity checked on every session, in line with zero trust.

3Key protection

Gateway keys held in an HSM.

4Measure

Track latency, throughput and handshake sizes before scaling.

title: Crypto-agility: designing a PKI that survives the post-quantum transition
sum: A PKI built around one algorithm will need to be rebuilt. A crypto-agile PKI can add post-quantum algorithms, run hybrid certificates and retire old keys without disrupting every relying system.
body: In brief. Crypto-agility is the ability to change algorithms, key sizes and certificate profiles through configuration and planned operations, not redevelopment. For certificate authorities, banks and governments it is the difference between a managed post-quantum transition and an emergency.
Five properties of an agile PKI

Algorithm-neutral design

Profiles and policies that name algorithms as parameters.

HSM support

HSMs that support or can be upgraded to ML-DSA and ML-KEM.

Parallel hierarchies

Classical, hybrid and post-quantum CAs can run side by side.

Automated lifecycle

Short-lived certificates and automated renewal make rotation routine.

Inventory and policy

Every certificate and relying system is known and owned.
Questions to ask your vendors

CA software
  • Which post-quantum and hybrid profiles are supported today?
  • How are new algorithms added?
HSMs
  • Firmware roadmap for ML-DSA and ML-KEM
  • Performance with larger keys and signatures
Relying systems
  • Can clients validate larger certificates and new OIDs?
  • What breaks first?

title: Post-quantum migration starts with a crypto inventory: a 90-day plan
sum: You cannot migrate what you cannot see. A cryptographic inventory tells you where RSA and elliptic-curve keys live, which data must stay secret longest, and where to start with post-quantum protection.
body: In brief. NIST published its first post-quantum standards in August 2024: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). NIST's draft transition guidance (IR 8547) proposes deprecating today's quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035. Large organizations need most of that time just to find and replace their cryptography.
The 90-day plan

1Days 1-30: discover

Scan certificates, TLS endpoints, code, libraries, HSMs and partner links; record algorithms and key sizes.

2Days 31-60: rank

Score each system by data lifetime, exposure and how hard it is to change.

3Days 61-75: design

Choose target profiles, hybrid options and vendor requirements.

4Days 76-90: pilot

Protect one high-value flow with hybrid key exchange and report results.
What the inventory should record

Where
  • Applications, devices, HSMs, cloud services, partners
What
  • Algorithm, key length, certificate, library and version
Why it matters
  • Data sensitivity and how long it must remain secret
  • Owner and change difficulty

title: Remote signing explained: CSC API, SCAL2 and sole control in plain English
sum: Remote signing standards sound complex, but the idea is simple: the key stays in a certified server, and only the signer can unlock it for a specific document. Here is how the pieces fit.
body: In brief. With remote signing the signer's private key is held by a trust service provider in an HSM. The Cloud Signature Consortium (CSC) API is the common interface that applications use to request signatures. SCAL2 is the strongest sole-control level: the signer's authorization is checked inside a certified Signature Activation Module before the key is used.
The flow

1Prepare

The application computes the document hash.

2Authorize

The signer approves on their phone, bound to that specific hash.

3Activate

The Signature Activation Module verifies the authorization inside the secure boundary.

4Sign

The HSM signs the hash; the signature returns to the application.
SCAL1 vs. SCAL2

SCAL1

The server is trusted to check the signer's authentication. Suitable for advanced signatures.

SCAL2

Authorization data is verified inside the SAM and linked to the exact data to be signed. Required for qualified remote signatures.

title: Passkeys for banking: FIDO2 beyond the login screen
sum: Passkeys remove phishable passwords and OTPs from login. Their bigger value for banks is authorizing payments, call-center identity and branch transactions with the same phishing-resistant credential.
body: In brief. A passkey is a FIDO2 credential bound to the bank's domain, so it cannot be phished onto a fake site. Used only for login it solves part of the problem. Used for every channel and every high-risk action it becomes the bank's single authentication layer.
Four channels, one credential

App and web login

No passwords or SMS OTPs to steal.

Payment authorization

Amount and payee shown and signed, meeting dynamic-linking requirements.

Call center

The customer approves an identity check in the app instead of answering security questions.

Branch and partners

The same credential confirms identity at a counter or a partner service.
Design decisions

Synced or device-bound

Synced passkeys are convenient; device-bound keys give stronger assurance for high-value actions.

Recovery

Account recovery is the new weak point and needs identity proofing, not an SMS.

Risk signals

Combine the passkey with device and session risk.

title: Custom cryptography inside an HSM: when you need it and how to deploy it safely
sum: Most projects use an HSM through standard APIs. Some, such as remote signing activation, national schemes and early post-quantum work, need code running inside the HSM's protected boundary. Here is when that makes sense.
body: In brief. Running custom code inside an HSM keeps sensitive logic, not only keys, within the certified boundary. It is powerful but costly: every vendor has its own SDK, certification scope changes, and upgrades need care.
When custom code is justified

Signature activation

A Signature Activation Module checks the signer's authorization inside the secure boundary before using the key.

National or sector algorithms

Algorithms or protocols the vendor does not ship.

Post-quantum pilots

Early testing of new algorithms before vendor firmware is available.

Sensitive business logic

Rules that must not be visible or changeable on the host.
How to do it safely

1Prefer standard APIs

Use PKCS #11 or vendor features first.

2Isolate the code

Keep custom modules small and independently reviewed.

3Plan certification

Agree with your auditor how the custom code affects the certified configuration.

4Design for upgrades

Version, sign and test modules against each firmware release.

title: What is an HSM? A 2026 buyer's guide for banks, CAs and governments
sum: A hardware security module protects the keys behind payments, certificates, signatures and national identity. Choosing one is a long-term decision about certification, performance, operations and the post-quantum path.
body: In brief. An HSM is a tamper-resistant device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys so they never appear in clear outside it. Banks, certificate authorities and governments use HSMs because their regulators and auditors require evidence that keys are protected by certified hardware.
Three families of HSM

General-purpose HSM

PKI, TLS, code signing, database encryption and application keys.

Payment HSM

PIN processing, card issuing and payment keys, certified to PCI PTS HSM.

Trust service HSM

Qualified signatures and seals, certified to Common Criteria EN 419 221-5 for eIDAS use.
Questions to ask before you buy

Certification
  • FIPS 140-3 level and certificate status
  • Common Criteria EN 419 221-5 where qualified services are planned
  • PCI PTS HSM for payment use
Performance and scale
  • Signatures per second for your key types
  • Clustering, high availability and disaster recovery
Post-quantum
  • ML-KEM and ML-DSA support or a firmware roadmap
  • Hybrid operation during migration
Operations
  • Remote management and key ceremonies
  • Deployment model: appliance, cloud or HSM as a service
  • Custom code support when you need it

title: eSeal for e-invoices and e-documents: authenticating the organization, not the person
sum: Invoices, statements, certificates and API responses are issued by organizations, often by machines, at high volume. An electronic seal proves where a document came from and that it has not changed.
body: In brief. A signature binds a person to a document. A seal binds an organization to it. For automated documents such as e-invoices, bank statements, academic certificates and government notices, the seal is the right tool: it proves origin and integrity without implying that a named person approved each copy.
Where eSeals fit

E-invoices and receipts

Issuer authenticity and tamper evidence at scale.

Statements and certificates

Customers and third parties can verify a PDF without calling the issuer.

APIs and data exchange

Sealed payloads prove which system produced the data.

Archives

Seals plus timestamps keep documents verifiable for years.
Designing a sealing service

1Certificate

An organizational certificate from a trusted CA.

2Key protection

Seal keys held in an HSM, with access limited to approved systems.

3Throughput

Batch and API sealing sized for peak volumes.

4Validation

Long-term validation data and timestamps embedded in the document.

title: Remote signing in Vietnam: when a cloud signature carries full legal weight
sum: Remote signing lets customers sign from any phone without a USB token. Whether that signature holds up depends on four things: the certificate, the signing device, sole control and the evidence trail.
body: In brief. Vietnam's Law on Electronic Transactions 2023 and Decree 23/2025/ND-CP on electronic signatures and trust services give digital signatures from licensed providers the same legal effect as handwritten signatures and set the rules for trust services, including remote signing. The legal weight of a cloud signature then comes from how it is produced.
Four tests a remote signature must pass

1The right certificate

Issued by a licensed public CA after proper identity proofing.

2A certified signing device

The private key lives in a certified HSM or remote signing device, never in an app.

3Sole control

Only the signer can activate the key, through strong authentication tied to the specific document.

4Evidence

Every step, from identity proof to signature activation, is logged and timestamped.
Where projects go wrong

Keys in software

A server that signs with keys in files cannot show sole control.

Weak activation

An SMS OTP alone is a thin basis for a high-value signature.

Missing evidence

Without logs and timestamps, a disputed signature is hard to defend.

title: Biometric checks for bank transfers in Vietnam: what Decision 2345 fixed, and where fraud moved next
sum: Vietnam's biometric rule for large transfers cut a classic fraud pattern sharply. Fraudsters adapted by targeting the genuine customer instead of the credentials. The next layer of defense is the device and the session.

sources.name: Báo Đầu tư - Fraud transactions down 50% after one month

body: In brief. Since 1 July 2024, SBV Decision 2345/QD-NHNN has required biometric verification against the chip ID card or VNeID for online transfers above VND 10 million, or above VND 20 million in total per day. Reported fraud cases fell by about half in the first month. Circular 77/2025, applicable from 1 March 2026, adds presentation-attack detection to ISO/IEC 30107 Level 2 and blocking of rooted or jailbroken devices.
What the rule fixed

Stolen credentials

A password and OTP are no longer enough to move large sums.

Mule accounts opened with fake IDs

Biometrics matched to the chip ID make synthetic identities harder.

Account takeover on a new phone

A new device must pass biometric enrolment first.
Where fraud moved next

1Social engineering

Victims are persuaded to authorize the transfer themselves.

2Split transfers

Amounts are kept below thresholds across several accounts.

3Remote control

Malware and screen sharing operate the session after the face check.

4Deepfakes and injection

Attackers try to beat the biometric step itself.

  • Binding the customer to a trusted device
  • Detecting remote control, overlays and emulators
Session
  • Behavioral signals and call-state awareness
  • Risk scoring for new payees and unusual amounts
Network
  • Graph analysis of mule chains
  • Sharing confirmed mule accounts across banks

sum: Since 1 January 2026, Vietnam's Personal Data Protection Law has set stricter rules for biometric data, consent and penalties. Banks and fintechs must keep fighting fraud while handling identity data more carefully.

sources.name: Hà Tĩnh provincial portal - Law in force from 1/1/2026
PwC Vietnam - New rules on personal data protection

body: In brief. Law No. 91/2025/QH15 on Personal Data Protection took effect on 1 January 2026, with detailed guidance in Decree 356/2025/ND-CP. It replaces the earlier decree-based regime with a law, treats biometric data as sensitive, and introduces revenue-based penalties for the most serious violations.
What it means for identity and fraud teams

Biometrics are sensitive data

Purpose and minimization

Impact assessments

Vendors and processors

Contracts with eKYC, cloud and analytics providers must reflect processor obligations.
Fraud prevention still has room

Detecting fraud and protecting customers are legitimate purposes, but they must be designed in rather than assumed. Device signals, behavioral data and shared fraud indicators should be collected with defined purposes, pseudonymized where possible, and retained only as long as needed.

title: Accepting EUDI Wallet credentials: five questions relying parties must answer first
sum: Member states must offer EU Digital Identity Wallets from late 2026, and regulated private services must accept them by the end of 2027. For banks and telecoms, the hard part is on the relying-party side.
body: In brief. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, private relying parties that are required by law to use strong user authentication, including banks, must accept the EUDI Wallet at the user's request within the timeline set by the regulation, which runs to the end of 2027. Acceptance is not a login button. It is a new trust relationship with every wallet and issuer in the EU.
The five questions

1Are we registered?

Relying parties register with their member state and receive access certificates that the wallet checks.

2What exactly do we ask for?

Requests must be limited to attributes registered for the stated purpose.

3Can we verify every issuer?

Credential checks depend on trusted lists and revocation status.

4Which journeys change?

Onboarding, login, payment authorization and signing each need a design decision.

5Where does the evidence go?

Logs must prove what was requested, presented and relied on.
Common mistakes

Treating it as SSO

Wallet presentations are cryptographic proofs, not redirects to an identity provider.

Over-asking

Requesting full identity data when an age or residency attribute would do.

Ignoring signing

The wallet can also create qualified electronic signatures, which changes document journeys.

title: PSD3 and PSR after the Council vote: what changes for banks inside and outside the EU
sum: The EU's new payment rules move a large share of fraud liability onto payment providers and pull platforms and telecom operators into fraud prevention. Banks outside Europe should read them as a preview.

sources.name: Lovguiden - Commission accepts Council position (3 Nov 2026)

body: Where things stand. After the provisional political agreement of 27 November 2025, the Council adopted its first-reading position in October 2026 and the European Commission accepted it on 3 November 2026. European Parliament second-reading approval is pending. Application is expected around 2028.
Five changes that matter for fraud

Payee verification for all transfers

Name and account checks before a credit transfer is sent, extending the approach already used for euro instant payments.

Impersonation refunds

Customers tricked by someone posing as their bank can claim a refund in defined cases.

Fraud data sharing

Payment providers may share fraud indicators with each other under clear data-protection safeguards.

Platforms and telecoms

Online platforms and electronic communications providers are expected to cooperate on removing fraudulent content and spoofed calls.

Stronger SCA rules

Clarified strong customer authentication, accessibility for all customers and limits on outsourcing it.
Why banks outside the EU should care

Regulators in Asia, Latin America and Africa watch Brussels closely. The pattern is familiar: first mandatory payee checks, then shared fraud data, then a shift of liability toward the institution that could have stopped the payment. title: Deepfake selfies and injection attacks: why liveness alone no longer proves presence
sum: Liveness detection was built to catch photos and masks held up to a camera. Today's attackers skip the camera entirely and inject synthetic video into the capture pipeline. Remote onboarding needs a wider defense.
body: In brief. Presentation attack detection (PAD) tests what is shown to the camera. An injection attack replaces the camera feed itself with a deepfake or replayed video, using virtual cameras, emulators or hooked apps. ETSI TS 119 461 now expects identity proofing services to consider both.
Two different attacks

Presentation attacks

A printed photo, a screen replay or a mask is shown to a real camera. Tested under ISO/IEC 30107-3.

Injection attacks

Synthetic or replayed video is fed into the app as if it came from the camera. Addressed by CEN/TS 18099 and by device and app integrity controls.
Where onboarding gets beaten

1Virtual camera

Software presents a deepfake stream as a webcam.

2Emulator or rooted phone

The capture app runs in an environment the attacker controls.

3Hooked app

Instrumentation tools swap frames after capture.

4Document side

A genuine stolen ID is paired with a synthetic face.
A layered defense

Capture integrity
  • Detect virtual cameras, emulators, hooking and rooted devices
  • Bind the capture to the app session and device
Biometric strength
  • PAD tested to ISO/IEC 30107-3
  • Injection detection aligned with CEN/TS 18099
  • Face match against the chip in the identity document where possible
Evidence and process
  • Keep the evidence an auditor will ask for
  • Risk-based escalation to manual review
  • Repeat checks at account recovery, not only onboarding

title: Remote-access scams and screen-sharing malware: the 2026 playbook against mobile banking
sum: The most damaging mobile fraud no longer breaks the bank's security. It takes over the customer's session from inside the phone. Here is how the playbook works and what stops it.
body: In brief. Fraudsters have shifted from stealing passwords to steering the victim's own phone. A call or message creates urgency, the victim installs a screen-sharing tool or a fake app, and the attacker watches or drives the banking session in real time. Strong login and biometrics do not help when the genuine customer is the one unlocking the app.
How the playbook runs

1Pretext

A call or message impersonates the bank, police, a courier or a tax office.

2Install

The victim is talked into a remote-access tool or a sideloaded app that requests Accessibility permissions.

3Watch

The attacker sees OTPs, balances and the screen as the customer logs in.

4Drive

Overlays and automated taps move money while the victim is kept on the phone.
Why existing controls miss it

The customer authenticates

Passwords, OTPs and face checks all succeed, because the real customer performs them.

Legitimate tools

Many remote-access apps are legitimate products, so blocklists alone are fragile.

Time pressure

The fraud completes in minutes, often before the customer realizes.
What works in 2026

In the app
  • Detect active screen sharing, screen recording and remote-control sessions
  • Detect Accessibility services that can read or tap the screen
  • Block overlays on sensitive screens and protect OTP fields
In the risk engine
  • Combine device signals with call state, new payee, amount and session behavior
  • Step up or hold first-time payees during a suspicious session
  • Score the device, not only the user
In operations
  • Short cooling-off periods for high-risk transfers
  • A fast path for customers to freeze their account
  • Share confirmed mule accounts across institutions where the law allows

title: Poisoned third-party JavaScript is now an iOS exploit channel: what banks should check now
sum: Researchers found compromised third-party scripts on major websites quietly routing iPhone visitors to exploit kits. Banks run the same kind of scripts in web banking and in-app WebViews. Here is what to check this week.
body: In brief. Research published on 17 November 2026 reports that poisoned third-party JavaScript on at least 21 major websites, including well-known news, collaboration and SaaS brands, sent iOS visitors to the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The attackers did not breach the websites themselves; they compromised analytics, widget and content vendors whose scripts those sites load. Banks load the same categories of scripts, so the lesson applies directly to web banking, onboarding pages and in-app WebViews.
What happened

According to Zimperium's write-up of the research, attackers modified JavaScript served by third-party vendors. Any site that embedded those scripts delivered the malicious code to its own visitors, from a domain the visitor and the browser both trusted.

The script profiled the device and, for iPhones on vulnerable versions, redirected the browser to exploit infrastructure. The report links the Coruna kit to iOS 15.x through 17.2.1, including a WebKit memory-corruption flaw (CVE-2022-48503), and the DarkSword kit to iOS 18.4 through 18.7.2. The chain moves from device profiling to code execution, sandbox escape and clean-up of forensic traces.

1Vendor compromised

An analytics, widget or content provider's script is modified.

2Trusted site serves it

Every page that embeds the script now delivers the attack.

3Device profiled

The script checks platform and iOS version silently.

4Exploit, implant, clean-up

Vulnerable iPhones are sent to a WebKit exploit and sandbox escape; traces are then removed.
Why this matters for banks

Most banks have spent years hardening their own servers. This campaign shows that the weakest point can be a script the bank did not write and rarely reviews. Login, onboarding and payment pages often carry tag managers, analytics, chat widgets, A/B testing tools and session replay. Mobile apps frequently open marketing pages, help centres or partner journeys in a WebView that loads the same scripts.

If a compromised device then opens the banking app, the bank is no longer dealing with a stranger on the internet. It is dealing with its own customer, on a device that may be under the attacker's control.
Why traditional defenses miss it

Trusted domains

The script arrives from a domain already allowed by web filters and content security policies.

Short windows

Supply-chain tampering can last hours or days, between scans and pen tests.

Out of view

Network and DNS controls see a normal page load; the exploit runs inside the browser on the customer's phone.
Ten checks for this week

Web journeys
  • List every third-party script on login, onboarding and payment pages
  • Remove what is not essential from those pages
  • Use Subresource Integrity and a strict Content Security Policy for what remains
  • Monitor script changes and alert on new sources
PCI DSS v4.0 requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 already expect an inventory, authorisation and change detection for payment-page scripts.
Mobile apps
  • Restrict WebViews to an allowlist of domains
  • Do not expose JavaScript bridges to untrusted content
  • Open marketing and partner content in the system browser, not inside the app
Device and risk
  • Read the OS version at session start and step up or limit high-value actions on vulnerable versions
  • Prompt customers to update iOS in-app
  • Feed device integrity signals into the fraud engine
How SAVIS helps

RASP+ protects the banking app at runtime and reports tampering, hooking and jailbreak indicators that commonly follow a successful device compromise. Device Intelligence adds OS version, integrity and risk signals to every session, and Fraud Prevention & Risk Management turns those signals into a decision: allow, step up, limit or block. Together they let a bank act on the device it is actually talking to, rather than on the assumption that the device is clean.

title: AI against AI: how banks and enterprises defend against deepfakes, synthetic identities and AI-driven fraud
sum: Generative AI has made fraud cheaper, faster and more convincing. Banks now need AI on defense too: liveness and deepfake detection, device and behavior signals, and an AI-assisted SOC.
body: In brief. Fraudsters use generative AI to fake faces, voices, documents and entire video meetings. Rules written for yesterday's fraud miss it. The answer is layered: prove the person is live and real, trust the device and the session, bind every payment to the customer, and let AI help analysts see the real threats first. Vietnam's Law on Artificial Intelligence, in force since 1 March 2026, and the EU AI Act add governance duties for AI used in finance.
What has changed

Deepfakes at scale

Face-swap and voice-clone tools are cheap and good enough to pass weak selfie checks and to impersonate executives on video calls.

Synthetic identities

Real and invented data are combined into identities that pass basic KYC, build history and then cash out.

Injection attacks

Instead of holding a fake to the camera, attackers inject video straight into the app with emulators and virtual cameras.

Social engineering, automated

Language models write convincing messages in any language and keep conversations going with thousands of victims at once.

Reported losses show the scale. In early 2024 a finance employee at the engineering firm Arup transferred about US$25 million after a video call in which every other participant was a deepfake. In the United States, FinCEN issued an alert in November 2024 asking banks to watch for deepfake media in fraud schemes. In Vietnam, the State Bank has required biometric checks against chip-based ID for larger online transfers since 1 July 2024, which makes liveness and anti-spoofing a front-line control.
Five layers of defense

1Prove the person

Passive liveness and deepfake detection at onboarding and at high-risk moments, designed for ISO/IEC 30107-3 presentation-attack detection.

2Trust the device

Device intelligence flags emulators, rooted phones, virtual cameras, remote-access tools and SIM swaps before login or payment.

3Protect the app

Runtime self-protection stops hooking, tampering and overlay attacks that feed fake video or steal credentials.

4Bind the payment

Strong customer authentication and transaction signing tie every amount and payee to the customer's key.

5Watch with AI

An AI-assisted SOC correlates fraud, device and security signals and ranks them so analysts act on real threats first.
Governing the AI you use

title: AI security for government, telecom and smart infrastructure: from AI SOC to trusted devices
sum: Cities, networks and factories now run on connected devices and AI. Securing them means trusted identities for every device, zero-trust access, and an AI-assisted SOC that can keep up.
body: In brief. Governments, telecom operators and industry are connecting millions of devices and adding AI to cameras, networks and production lines. Each device is an entry point, and each AI model is a new asset to protect. The priorities are the same everywhere: give every device a trusted identity, verify every access, protect AI models and data, and monitor everything with AI-assisted operations.
Where the risk sits

GovernmentDigital public services, chatbots, document AIIdentity fraud, data leakage, prompt injection in citizen-facing assistants

Five controls that matter most

1Identity for every device

Device certificates and protected keys so only genuine sensors, cameras and gateways can connect.

2Signed firmware and secure boot

Devices run only code you approved, and updates cannot be swapped in transit.

3Zero-trust access

Every user and device is verified on every request, instead of trusting the network.

4Protect AI models and data

title: Post-quantum banking: what NIST's final transition timeline means for banks and enterprises
sum: NIST's final IR 8547 sets the end date for RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. Banks that hold long-lived data and run long-lived systems need to start migrating now.
body: In brief. A large enough quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, which protect payments, online banking, certificates and signed records today. Attackers can already record encrypted traffic and decrypt it later. NIST published the post-quantum standards in August 2024 and, in its final IR 8547 of October 2026, set the timeline: classical public-key algorithms are deprecated from 2031 and disallowed after 31 December 2035. The EU roadmap asks for the first steps by the end of 2026 and high-risk systems migrated by 2030.
The timeline at a glance

WhenMilestone
August 2024NIST publishes FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA).
June 2025EU Member States publish a coordinated roadmap: start by end of 2026, high-risk use cases by 2030, as much as feasible by 2035.
October 2026NIST final IR 8547: RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA and (EC)DH deprecated from 2031, disallowed after 31 December 2035; hybrid ML-KEM key exchange recommended now.
2030US federal high-impact systems move key establishment to post-quantum cryptography.
2035Classical public-key algorithms disallowed under NIST guidance.
Why banks cannot wait

Harvest now, decrypt later

Customer data, contracts and archives must stay secret for 10 to 20 years, longer than the quantum timeline.

Long-lived systems

HSMs, cards, ATMs and core platforms bought today will still run in 2035.

Many dependencies

Card schemes, payment switches, CAs, cloud providers and vendors must all move together.

Signatures that must last

Signed contracts and records need to stay verifiable for their full retention period.
A five-step migration

1Discover

Build a cryptographic bill of materials: every algorithm, key, certificate and protocol in use.

2Rank

Prioritize by data lifetime, exposure and system replacement cycles.

3Make it agile

Switch algorithms by policy instead of rewriting applications.

4Go hybrid

Deploy hybrid ML-KEM key exchange and hybrid certificates alongside classical ones.

5Migrate and prove

Move system by system, starting with high-risk ones, and report progress to the board and regulators.
How SAVIS helps

The Quantum Readiness Program and Crypto Agility start with discovery and a roadmap; PQC Suite and Quantum Safe Gateway add hybrid post-quantum protection to existing systems; GP HSM, Payment HSM and KMS protect keys; and Quantum Vault and Quantum Safe Storage protect long-lived data. Pilots can be tested in the SAVIS Quantum PQC Lab.

title: VietNam’s draft digital identity law: who is affected, and how it compares globally
sum: The draft before the National Assembly would put VNeID, licensed identity providers, three authentication levels and mandatory identity linking in eleven sectors into one law. Here is what it says, who must prepare, and how it compares internationally.
body: In brief. The Ministry of Public Security presented the draft Law on Electronic Identification and Authentication to the 2nd session of the 16th National Assembly on 26 October 2026, and deputies debated it in plenary on 4 November. It is expected to be voted on before the session closes on 21 November 2026. The draft is still changing — this analysis follows the published draft and official reporting as of 17 November 2026.
The framework at a glance
What the draft does

One legal framework

Brings electronic identity, authentication, the national platform and private identity services under one law (8 chapters, 46 articles in the version presented in October).

Five kinds of identity

Not only people and organisations: also goods and physical assets; data, software and digital services; events and transactions; and locations and spaces.

Two ways to identify

The State runs identification for core, sensitive and high-risk objects; qualified organisations may build their own identification systems for the rest.

Three ways to authenticate

Centralised (through the identity provider), intermediary (through an authentication service) and independent (the relying party verifies credentials itself).

Three authentication levels

One factor; two factors (knowledge and possession); and at least two factors including a biometric. Deputies asked for minimum levels set by transaction risk, and for Level 3 to require a hardware-bound factor such as the chip in the citizen ID card.

National platform

A national identification and authentication database, the VNeID app, a validity-management system and a national gateway. The national app can also issue digital signatures.

Identity service providers

Conditions on legal status, finances, technology, staff, data protection, cybersecurity, connectivity and liability insurance — with a transition period for existing providers and a regulatory sandbox.

Cross-border

Mutual recognition of foreign electronic identities by treaty or agreement. Deputies asked to limit recognition to an approved list and to clarify liability.
Mandatory identity linking: the sectors affected

Reporting on the 4 November debate cites eleven sectors in which online transactions would have to be authenticated with, and linked to, the national electronic identity. Ministers could add other high-risk fields.
BankingPayment intermediariesE-walletsSecuritiesCrypto-assetsTelecommunicationsPostal servicesE-commerceHealthcareOnline gamesDomain names

SectorWhat changesWhat to prepare
Banks & paymentsCustomer authentication tied to the national identity; risk-based minimum levelsMap journeys to Levels 1–3; chip-card and face checks for high-risk transactions; consent records
Securities & crypto-assetsIdentity linking for account opening and tradingVNeID-based onboarding; strong authentication for orders and withdrawals
Telecom & postalSubscriber and sender identity linked to national identityRe-verification at scale; data minimisation in shared attributes
E-commerce & gamesLinking for buyers, sellers and playersLight-touch flows with the right level per transaction; age and fraud checks
HealthcarePatients identified electronically for examination and treatmentHospital and insurance systems connected through a secure integration layer
Identity & trust providersLicensing conditions, insurance, connection to the national system, data stored in VietNamGap assessment against the conditions; security certification; a transition plan
What deputies are still debating

• Scope: business groups warned that “transactions” could cover nearly all everyday commerce; deputies asked to tie linking to risk.
  • Privacy: consent that names the data, purpose, recipient and duration; access logs people can review; disclosing only the attributes a transaction needs.
  • Tracing: who may request and approve tracing of a digital identity should be in the law, not left to a decree.
  • Deepfakes: a reported case of deepfakes defeating biometric checks on nearly 1,000 bank accounts was cited to argue for hardware-bound Level 3.
  • Re-use of data: no re-submission of data the State already holds; existing VNeID accounts and identifiers carried over.
How VietNam compares

Main legal basisModelPrivate identity providersAssurance levelsIs use mandatory?

SingaporeNo single digital ID statute; Electronic Transactions Act, PDPAGovernment-run Singpass and MyinfoBusinesses integrate Singpass rather than run their own national identitySet by Singpass authentication methodsVoluntary; Singpass Digital IC accepted by all government agencies since November 2021
IndiaAadhaar Act 2016 (amended 2019); DPDP Act 2023Central biometric identity (UIDAI) with authentication APIsSince 2025, approved private entities may use Aadhaar authentication for specified purposesOTP, biometric and face authenticationRequired for government benefits; private use limited by law and court rulings
AustraliaDigital ID Act 2024 (from 1 December 2024)Government Digital ID System plus an accreditation schemeAccredited private providers; the system opens to the private sector in phasesDefined in accreditation rulesVoluntary; an alternative to Digital ID must generally be offered
New ZealandDigital Identity Services Trust Framework Act 2023 (from 1 July 2024)Opt-in trust frameworkAccredited providers under the Trust Framework AuthoritySet in the trust framework rulesVoluntary
Five takeaways

1Broader scope

VietNam’s draft covers objects, data and transactions — far wider than identity laws that cover people and organisations.

2Mandatory where others are voluntary

Most peers rely on accreditation and choice; the draft makes linking compulsory in eleven sectors.

3Risk-based levels

Three levels line up with eIDAS low/substantial/high and NIST assurance; mapping them early eases cross-border recognition.

4Hardware-bound Level 3

The chip ID card plus face and liveness checks is the strongest answer to deepfakes.

5Privacy by design

Consent, minimal attributes and reviewable logs are where VietNam can match EU and Singapore practice.
How SAVIS helps

SAVIS connects the pieces the law brings together: VNeID Integration and ID Verification for identity proofing with the chip ID card; TrustCA eKYC Biometric and TrustCA Remote Signing for certificates and signatures; Consent Management for consent and access logs; and SAVIS Digital Integration Platform for secure, FAPI 2.0-protected data exchange. title: Quantum-safe government and telecom networks: PQC, QKD and national PKI
sum: National PKI, eID, government networks and telecom backbones must stay trusted for decades. Post-quantum cryptography protects them everywhere; QKD adds protection on selected links.
body: In brief. Governments and telecom operators run the longest-lived trust infrastructure in a country: national root CAs, ID cards, e-passports, government networks and the backbone that carries everyone's traffic. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is the main path to quantum safety because it runs in software and existing hardware. Quantum key distribution (QKD) can add physics-based key exchange on high-value fiber links. Most national strategies combine both under a crypto-agility plan.
PQC and QKD compared

Post-quantum cryptographyQuantum key distribution
What it isNew mathematical algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)Keys shared using quantum states of light
Where it runsAnywhere: servers, HSMs, phones, cards, IoTDedicated fiber or free-space links between sites
DistanceUnlimitedLimited per link; trusted nodes or repeaters for longer routes
AuthenticationBuilt in (signatures)Needs a separate authenticated channel, often PQC
Best useEverything, as the defaultSelected high-value links such as data-center interconnects
Priorities by sector

National PKI and eID

Plan hybrid and post-quantum root and issuing CAs; certificates and ID cards issued today live 5 to 10 years.

Government networks

Hybrid key exchange on VPNs and inter-agency links; QKD pilots on core links between data centers.

Telecom backbones

Quantum-safe transport (for example OTN and IPsec) and SIM and core-network keys planned with industry groups such as the GSMA.

IoT and smart cities

Choose devices whose firmware can be updated to post-quantum algorithms over their full service life.

Timelines are converging. The EU roadmap asks Member States to start by the end of 2026 and to protect high-risk use cases by 2030. In the United States, NIST's final IR 8547 disallows classical public-key algorithms after 2035, and the NSA's CNSA 2.0 sets earlier dates for national security systems. In Vietnam, the national cryptographic algorithm MKV and international PQC standards are both part of the conversation on trust services, as discussed at the July 2026 Hanoi conference on post-quantum PKI hosted by NEAC, SAVIS and DigiCert.
How SAVIS helps

SAVIS builds and operates National PKI and trust services, provides PQC Suite, Crypto Agility and Quantum Safe Gateway for migration, and delivers QKD and Quantum Communication pilots with technology partners. The SAVIS Quantum PQC Lab runs a QKD-secured 400 Gbit/s OTN testbed for proofs of concept.

Sources: NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026); NIS Cooperation Group PQC roadmap (June 2025); NSA CNSA 2.0 guidance; SAVIS press release on the July 2026 conference “Shaping the Future of PKI Infrastructure”.

title: Side-channel attacks: why the chip matters as much as the algorithm for cards, tokens and HSMs
sum: A strong algorithm can still leak its key through timing, power or electromagnetic emissions. EUCLEAK showed that even certified secure elements can be affected. Here is what banks should ask for.
body: In brief. Side-channel attacks (SCA) do not break the mathematics. They measure how a device behaves while it computes, such as its timing, power draw or electromagnetic emissions, and recover the secret key from those signals. Cards, tokens, phones and HSMs that hold bank and customer keys are the targets. In September 2024, the EUCLEAK research showed that an electromagnetic side channel in a widely used secure-element library could reveal ECDSA keys, after about 14 years and many high-level certifications.
The main attack families

TypeWhat is measuredTypical targets
TimingHow long operations takeSoftware crypto, servers, TLS libraries
Power analysis (SPA/DPA)Power consumption during computationSmart cards, tokens, secure elements
Electromagnetic (EM)Emissions near the chipSecure elements, phones, IoT chips
Cache and micro-architecturalShared CPU resourcesCloud servers, laptops, phones
Fault injectionGlitches in voltage, clock or laserCards and secure elements (often combined with SCA)
Lessons from EUCLEAK

Certification is not forever

A flaw in the Infineon cryptographic library went unnoticed through about 80 Common Criteria evaluations.

Physical access still matters

The attack needed the device, specialist equipment and skills, which is why it suits targeted attacks on high-value keys.

Firmware must be updatable

Affected YubiKey 5 devices with firmware below 5.7 could not be patched and had to be replaced.

PQC needs it too

Post-quantum algorithms must also be implemented in constant time and with masking, as research such as KyberSlash (2024) showed.
What to ask your vendors

1Certified resistance

Common Criteria with AVA_VAN.5 for cards and secure elements; FIPS 140-3 or equivalent for HSMs.

2Tested against SCA

Evidence of non-invasive testing, for example to ISO/IEC 17825, and leakage assessment.

3Countermeasures

Constant-time code, masking, shuffling and fault detection, including for PQC.

4Updatability

A secure way to update firmware and switch algorithms during the device's life.

5Defense in depth

Keys in hardware, PIN or biometric unlock, and monitoring for cloned or misused credentials.
How SAVIS helps

SAVIS keeps keys inside hardware with GP HSM, Payment HSM and SAM Appliance, issues credentials on PKI Token, Crypto Bio Token and Smart Card PIV, and manages their lifecycle with Credential Management so affected devices can be found and replaced quickly. Crypto Agility helps switch algorithms when a weakness is found.
Sources: T. Roche (NinjaLab), “EUCLEAK”, IACR ePrint 2024/1380 and Yubico Security Advisory (September 2024); CVE-2024-45678; ISO/IEC 17825; Common Criteria AVA_VAN; KyberSlash research (2024).

title: Side-channel attacks on eID cards, SIMs, smart meters and IoT: protecting keys in the field
sum: Devices deployed in public places can be stolen, opened and measured. National ID, telecom and IoT programs need keys that resist side-channel and fault attacks for years.
body: In brief. ID cards, e-passports, SIMs, smart meters, cameras and industrial sensors spend years in the field, where an attacker can hold one in their hands. That makes them natural targets for side-channel and fault-injection attacks that extract keys or clone credentials. Programs at national scale need secure elements tested against these attacks, a unique key per device, and the ability to revoke and update when a weakness is found.
Why field devices are exposed

Physical access

Meters, kiosks, cameras and cards can be taken to a lab and measured for days.

Scale

One extracted shared key can compromise millions of devices; unique keys contain the damage.

Long lifetimes

eID cards last 5 to 10 years and meters 15 or more, longer than many crypto libraries stay unbroken.

Cheap chips

Low-cost microcontrollers often lack side-channel countermeasures unless a secure element is added.
Requirements by program

ProgramKey protections
eID cards and e-passportsSecure elements certified to Common Criteria with AVA_VAN.5; ICAO 9303 protocols; per-card keys
SIM and eSIMGSMA-certified secure elements and secure remote provisioning
Smart meters and IoTSecure element or certified MCU (for example SESIP); unique device certificates; signed firmware; ETSI EN 303 645 or IEC 62443
Kiosks and terminalsTamper detection that erases keys, secure boot and monitored access
Five design rules

1A secure element for every key

Never store long-term keys in general-purpose memory.

2One key per device

Diversified keys so one extraction does not open the fleet.

3Tamper response

Sensors that erase session keys and alert the SOC when a case is opened.

4Lifecycle control

Issue, renew and revoke certificates centrally; push signed firmware updates.

5Plan for PQC

Choose secure elements and firmware that can move to post-quantum algorithms implemented with side-channel countermeasures.
How SAVIS helps

SAVIS delivers national ID and credentials with National eID Trust, Smart Card PIV and Credential Management; device identity and signed firmware with IoT Device Security and National PKI; tamper-aware AI Camera Security and Smart Kiosk designs; and monitoring through the SAVIS AI SOC.
Sources: ISO/IEC 17825; Common Criteria AVA_VAN; GlobalPlatform SESIP; ICAO Doc 9303; ETSI EN 303 645; IEC 62443; EUCLEAK (IACR ePrint 2024/1380).

title: eIDAS and eIDAS 2.0: what businesses and organizations need to know
sum: eIDAS made electronic signatures valid across the EU. eIDAS 2.0 adds the European Digital Identity Wallet, new trust services and tougher rules for trust service providers.
body: In brief. Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, known as eIDAS, created one legal framework for electronic identification and trust services across all 27 EU Member States. It defines three levels of electronic signature, with the qualified electronic signature (QES) equal to a handwritten one. eIDAS 2.0, Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, in force since 20 May 2024, adds the European Digital Identity Wallet, new qualified trust services and stricter security and supervision duties for trust service providers.
What eIDAS is

Before eIDAS, each EU Member State had its own rules for electronic signatures. A signature valid in France was not necessarily recognized in Germany or Spain, which made cross-border transactions complex. The EU solved this with Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 on electronic identification, authentication and trust services (eIDAS), adopted on 23 July 2014 and applicable from 1 July 2016. As a regulation, it applies directly and uniformly in all 27 Member States without being transposed into national law.

A single digital market

Mutual recognition of electronic identities across the EU.

Legal certainty

Cross-border electronic transactions are legally valid and secure.

A framework of trust

Digital services rely on supervised Qualified Trust Service Providers (QTSPs).
Three levels of electronic signature

LevelRequirementsTypical usesLegal effect
Simple electronic signature (SES)Electronic data attached to other electronic data and used to sign; no specific technical standard.Accepting terms, ticking a box, typing a name in a form, confirming by email.Valid for basic contracts; cannot be refused as evidence only because it is electronic.
Advanced electronic signature (AES)Uniquely linked to and capable of identifying the signer; created with data under the signer's sole control; any later change to the document is detectable.Employment contracts, NDAs, commercial agreements, powers of attorney.High evidential value; recommended for important contracts.
Qualified electronic signature (QES)Meets all AES requirements; created with a qualified signature creation device (QSCD); based on a qualified certificate issued by a QTSP.Electronic notarization, large public tenders and other high-value documents.Equivalent to a handwritten signature (Article 25) and recognized in every Member State.
What eIDAS 2.0 changes

eIDAS was amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, published on 30 April 2024 and in force since 20 May 2024. Its centerpiece is the European Digital Identity Wallet (EUDI Wallet): every Member State must offer citizens and residents an app to store and present verified identity data and electronic attestations, such as ID cards, driving licenses, diplomas, certificates and other attested attributes. The wallets work across the whole EU, which makes identity checks and cross-border digital transactions simpler.

European Digital Identity Wallet

A wallet for every citizen and resident, usable for public and private services across the EU. See our analysis of the wallet deadlines in December 2026 and 2027.

Stricter rules for trust service providers

New requirements for cybersecurity, audits and supervision, business continuity and service availability.

New qualified trust services

Electronic archiving, electronic attestation of attributes and qualified electronic ledgers.

Stronger interoperability

A qualified electronic signature issued in one Member State is recognized in all others under the eIDAS framework.
Benefits for citizens, businesses and governments

Citizens

Easier access to public and private services through the wallet, simpler authentication, and more privacy and control over what is shared online.

Businesses

Simpler customer identity checks, lower operating costs and less fraud; EU-wide standards make cross-border trade and new digital services easier.

Governments

Better online public services, simpler identification, interoperable systems across Member States and less paperwork.
SAVIS and eIDAS 2.0

eIDAS 2.0 raises the bar for trust service providers worldwide. SAVIS has achieved eIDAS 2.0 certification for its TrustCA trust services: TrustCA Remote Signing, TrustCA Timestamp and electronic seals (eSeal). It is an important step in demonstrating SAVIS's technology, security and compliance with international standards for digital trust services. SAVIS also helps other organizations prepare with eIDAS 2.0 Readiness and Digital ID Wallet.
Talk to a SAVIS expert about qualified signatures and trust services →

title: From ministries to communes: connecting government services with FAPI 2.0 security
sum: Public services now run across ministries, provinces and communes. A shared integration platform — secured to the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile — lets them exchange data once, safely, and traceably.
body: A citizen applying for a service touches many systems: a ministry register, a provincial back office, a commune service desk and the app or portal they started from. When those systems cannot talk to each other, people are asked for the same documents again and again.

Since 1 July 2025 VietNam’s local government has worked in two tiers — province and commune. More services are now delivered close to residents, which makes reliable, secure data exchange between central and local systems more important than ever.
Why FAPI 2.0

FAPI 2.0 is the OpenID Foundation’s hardened profile of OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, first proven in open banking for high-value APIs. Citizen data deserves the same protection. The FAPI 2.0 Security Profile asks for:

• Pushed authorisation requests (PAR) so request parameters cannot be tampered with in the browser.
  • PKCE to bind the authorisation code to the client that asked for it.
  • Sender-constrained tokens with mutual TLS or DPoP, so a stolen token is useless to anyone else.
  • Strong client authentication with private_key_jwt or mutual TLS — a natural fit for certificates from the government PKI.
How SAVIS Digital Integration Platform applies it

• Central to local in one platform: ministries, national databases and the national data exchange platform on one side; provincial and commune systems on the other.
  • Service catalogue: agencies publish APIs and data once and reuse them everywhere.
  • FAPI 2.0 authorisation server: every agency application and citizen app is a registered client with sender-constrained tokens.
  • Consent and audit: each exchange is authorised, logged and traceable end to end.
  • Monitoring: health, usage and security dashboards for every agency and integration.
Four steps to get started

1. Inventory systems, APIs and the data each agency shares.
  2. Design the service catalogue and the security profile — FAPI 2.0 for sensitive data, simpler profiles for open data.
  3. Onboard the first agencies and clients, then scale to all ministries, provinces and communes.
  4. Operate and monitor around the clock.
Combined with the SAVIS SuperApp platform and SAVIS eGate, the platform lets residents start a service in one place and have it completed across every level of government.

title: EU Digital Identity Wallet: what changes on 24 December 2026 and 2027
sum: Every EU member state must offer a wallet by 24 December 2026; a year later, banks and telcos must accept it. Here is what each role must do.
body: eIDAS 2.0 fixes five weaknesses of the 2014 regulation: a fragmented market, a private sector left out, too few people with cross-border eID, logins tied to social networks rather than real identity, and uneven supervision of trust services.

Member states must provide at least one wallet, free for individuals, holding person identification data (PID) and attestations of attributes. Public bodies must accept the wallet for their services. Relying parties must register and ask only for the data they need.

Wallet providers must build in security, separate wallet data and never collect transaction history without consent. Trust service providers face new requirements, compliance audits and incident reporting. Users get selective disclosure, deletion, pseudonyms, a transaction history and qualified electronic signatures free of charge for personal use.
Four credential types — PID, PuB-EAA, QEAA and EAA — use SD-JWT VC and ISO mdoc, issued with OpenID4VCI and presented with OpenID4VP or ISO 18013-5.

Large-scale pilots (POTENTIAL, EWC, NOBID, DC4EU) have already tested bank account opening, SIM registration, mobile driving licences, qualified signatures, travel credentials, diplomas and health insurance cards.
SAVIS supports each role: verifiers and eKYC for relying parties, issuers for attributes, SAM Appliance as a remote QSCD and TrustCA as a QTSP.

title: 2.8 billion people still lack a digital ID they can use online

body: About 800 million people have no legal proof of identity, more than 400 million of them in sub-Saharan Africa, and 2.8 billion lack a digital ID they can use for online transactions (World Bank ID4D, 2025).

Only 89 countries — about 45% — have a government-recognised digital ID that can be verified remotely. The World Bank ID4D programme supports 49 countries, with more than USD 1.5 billion committed or planned in 35 of them.
McKinsey Global Institute estimates digital identity could unlock economic value equal to 3–13% of GDP by 2030.

Three gaps undermine digital trust: transactions hijacked through real-time phishing and SIM swaps; identities faked with forged documents and deepfakes; and cryptography at risk from future quantum computers, now that NIST has published FIPS 203, 204 and 205.

Countries choose centralised, federated or wallet-based models — often a mix. SAVIS products work in all three: as identity provider or OIDC bridge, FIDO2 strong authentication, HSM and PKI to sign credentials, and verifiers for banks.

title: Open-source national IDMS with MOSIP: modules, architecture and how SAVIS delivers it
sum: MOSIP gives countries an open, modular identity platform. Here is how its modules fit together, where ABIS, devices and PKI plug in, and the roles SAVIS plays in a MOSIP programme.
body: MOSIP (Modular Open Source Identity Platform) is an open-source platform for building foundational national identity systems. Countries own the software and choose their own vendors for biometrics, devices, hosting and integration — avoiding lock-in to a single supplier.

The MOSIP modules

Enrolment
  • Pre-registration portal
  • Registration client (operators, devices)
  • Registration processor (packet validation, de-duplication)
Identity core
  • ID repository (UIN, demographic and biometric records)
  • Key manager (keys, signatures, encryption)
  • Admin and partner management
Use of identity
  • ID authentication (1:1, OTP, biometrics)
  • eSignet — OIDC login for relying parties
  • Resident services portal
Credentials

Pluggable by design. MOSIP does not include its own biometric matcher or devices. It defines interfaces — the queue-based ABIS API, the biometric SDK and the secure biometric interface for devices — so certified vendors plug in.
Where SAVIS fits
Greenfield or brownfield

In a greenfield programme the country builds its first digital ID on MOSIP. In a brownfield programme MOSIP modules — often eSignet or Inji — are added to an existing ID system. SAVIS supports both: a full MOSIP IDMS, or individual components such as ABIS, eSignet integration or credential issuance on top of an existing register.
A typical delivery plan

1Assess

Legal framework, registers, enrolment network and connectivity.

2Design

Module selection, ABIS and device sizing, PKI and data-protection design.

3Pilot

Rapid pilot in one region, including the MOSIP test kits.

4Roll out

Mass enrolment, de-duplication and credential issuance.

5Operate

24/7 operations, security monitoring and capacity planning.
SAVIS MOSIP compliance testing is in progress. Sources: MOSIP documentation (ABIS integration, version 1.2.0); MOSIP Connect 2026 coverage, Biometric Update (February 2026).

title: Digital civil registration with OpenCRVS: from birth to identity
sum: OpenCRVS is an open-source civil registration system recognised as a Digital Public Good. How it works, how it connects to MOSIP and health systems, and what SAVIS adds.
body: Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) is the foundation of legal identity: a person who is not registered at birth often cannot get an ID, a passport, school enrolment or social protection later. OpenCRVS is an open-source system built to digitise this process, especially where offices are far apart and connectivity is poor.
How a vital event is processed

1Declare

Informant, field agent or health facility declares the event — online or offline.

2Validate

Registration agent checks the declaration and supporting documents.

3Register

Local registrar registers the event in the official record.

4Certify

Certificate printed and signed; certified copies issued later.

5Correct and verify

Approved corrections; third parties verify certificates.

Offline-first

Field agents declare events without a connection; data syncs later.

Multi-language

Forms, certificates and notifications in national languages.

Signed certificates

Digitally signed birth certificates; SMS when ready.

Real-time data

Completeness and timeliness dashboards for decision-makers.
Birth-to-ID with MOSIP
OpenCRVS integrates with MOSIP so civil registration and national identity form one lifecycle:

1Birth → UIN

Registering an eligible birth sends a packet through the MOSIP Packet Manager; once MOSIP confirms, the record is registered and a VID issued.

2eSignet checks

Informants and parents are authenticated with eSignet; their data pre-fills the form. A partner-specific token is stored instead of the UIN.

3Corrections

Approved corrections to shared fields send an updated packet to MOSIP.

4Death → deactivation

Registering a death flags the person's VID as deceased in MOSIP.
Who uses it. OpenCRVS is used in Nigeria and Madagascar, with pilots or programmes in Bangladesh, Mauritius, Cameroon and Niue, according to UNDP's Digital X catalogue.
What SAVIS adds

Implementation

Configuration of events, forms, roles, jurisdictions, certificates and languages.

Integration

MOSIP, national registers, health systems (FHIR), statistics and social protection.

Security

Certificate signing with SAVIS PKI and HSM, hardening, SOC monitoring.

Credentials

Birth certificates as verifiable credentials, or offline SAVIS CryptoID.

Hosting

Government data centre or cloud, including air-gapped installs.

Operations

Training, 24/7 support and legacy record migration.

What this means for programme owners

In mature markets the task is to modernise: move from cards and passwords to wallets, passkeys and remote qualified signatures, and get relying parties to accept them. In building and nascent markets the order matters: a deduplicated foundational register and a national PKI must come first, because every credential issued later inherits their assurance level.

title: Seven technology shifts in digital identity, 2026–2030
sum: Cards and passwords are giving way to wallets, passkeys, deepfake-resistant biometrics and post-quantum cryptography. Here is what changes at each layer — and which standards anchor it.
body: Digital identity is changing at every layer at once. The table summarises where most deployments are today, where they are heading between 2026 and 2030, and the standards that make the new approach interoperable.

Three implications

Design for the wallet

Issuers should be able to publish credentials over OpenID4VCI and verify them over OpenID4VP and ISO 18013-5 — whichever wallet the citizen uses.

Digital ID Wallet
Retire shared secrets

Passwords and SMS OTP are the main source of account takeover. Passkeys and hardware authenticators remove them.

FIDO2 Passwordless Identity
Plan the PQC migration now

Signing keys and long-lived credentials need a path to ML-DSA and ML-KEM. Start with a cryptographic inventory.

Crypto Agility
Sources: ISO/IEC, ICAO, W3C (VC 2.0, May 2025), NIST (SP 800-63-4, FIPS 203–205), ETSI, CEN, FIDO Alliance, OpenID Foundation.

title: The six-layer identity hierarchy: trust flows from the person up to the transaction
sum: Each layer of identity can only be trusted if the layer beneath it is. A practical model for designing identity systems — and where each SAVIS product fits.
body: Identity programmes often fail at the joins: a strong card issued from a weak enrolment, or a passkey bound to an account that was never properly verified. The identity hierarchy makes the dependencies explicit. Read it from the bottom up.

Identity server · SSO · pseudonyms in the wallet

Attestation issuers and verifiers

National eID · PKI · HSM signing of PID

Bottom-up rule. A transaction is only as trustworthy as the person, foundation, biography and context beneath it.
Products by layer

Person and foundation: SAVIS TrustOnboard and TrustCA eKYC Biometric prove a live person with presentation-attack detection to ISO/IEC 30107-3 Level 2; National eID Trust and National PKI bind that person to a state-issued identity whose keys stay in the HSM.

title: Digital public infrastructure: identity, data exchange and payments — tied together by wallets and a trust framework
sum: Digital ID, data exchange and digital payments are the three pillars of DPI. Wallets and a national trust framework are what make them work together for citizens and businesses.
body: Digital public infrastructure (DPI) is usually described as three pillars. In practice a fourth element — wallets and credentials — and a trust framework underneath decide whether the pillars connect or stay as silos.

Issuer · verifier

Trust framework and trust registry: the law, assurance levels and certification of participants; lists of authorised issuers, verifiers and wallets; the national PKI and HSMs. SAM Appliance and TrustCA provide this layer.

Citizens reach DPI through a wallet on the phone, self-service web portals and assisted enrolment points. Government agencies, banks and mobile wallets, telcos, and health, education and insurance providers sit on top as services. The design question is not which pillar to build first, but how each new service reuses the same identity, consent and trust registry.

title: How selective disclosure works: proving you are over 18 without showing your birth date
sum: SD-JWT VC and mdoc credentials are bound to the device and let the holder share one attribute at a time — while the verifier can still check the issuer's signature.
body: A verifiable credential has to satisfy two goals that look contradictory: share as little as possible, and still be provably genuine. Salted hashes make both possible.

1Issuance

The wallet generates a key pair in hardware and sends the public key with an attestation. The issuer hashes each attribute with a salt and signs with its key in the HSM. Several copies are issued to prevent linkability.

Issuer HSM
2Structure (SD-JWT VC)

Issuer-signed JWT with salted hashes of each attribute and the device key (cnf) · Disclosures: salt + name + value, only for the attributes chosen · Key-binding JWT: the wallet signs the nonce and verifier address.

3Presentation and checks

The verifier checks the issuer is on a Trusted List, the disclosed hashes match, the nonce is signed with the device key, the credential is not revoked (status list) and its own RP certificate is valid.

Verifier

Example — over 18. The wallet sends only the disclosure “over 18: true”: no birth date, address or document number. The verifier can still verify the issuer's signature because the hash of that disclosure is inside the signed part; undisclosed attributes stay private because their salts are never revealed.
mdoc credentials (ISO/IEC 18013-5) use the same principle: a table of salted hashes signed by the issuer.
SAVIS delivers both sides: issuer signing in SAM Appliance and verification components for relying parties in Digital ID Wallet.
Sources: IETF SD-JWT VC; ISO/IEC 18013-5; OpenID4VCI / VP; EUDI technical documentation (2025–2026).
