title: Peru: RENIEC issues the digital DNI on Perú Pass and opens the door to certified private wallets
sum: RENIEC is the source of identity truth; INDECOPI accredits trust services under IOFE; and from 31 July 2026 the digital DNI can live in other compliant wallets too.
body: Peru combines a strong civil registry with an accreditation-based trust-services regime. The result is an ecosystem where a single source of identity feeds public and private verifiers alike.

What is open: the DNId regulation allows other compliant wallets to coexist with Perú Pass; public and private verifiers must integrate RENIEC's tools; trust services are accredited by INDECOPI within IOFE.

For technology providers the opportunities are in the accredited roles — certification, registration and value-added services such as remote signing — and in verifier integration for banks and telcos. SAVIS technology such as TrustCA Remote Signing, Timestamp Authority (TSA) and Digital ID Wallet maps directly onto these roles.
Sources: RENIEC (RJ D000012-2026-RENIEC/JNAC; identidad.reniec.gob.pe); gob.pe; Biometric Update (August 2026); INDECOPI – IOFE.

title: Chile: chip ID card, digital ID on the phone, and ClaveÚnica as the identity broker
sum: SRCeI issues the chip card and digital ID; ClaveÚnica brokers access to 2,000+ services; accredited providers issue advanced signatures (FEA); and Law 21.719 raises the bar on consent and biometrics.
body: Chile's model separates roles cleanly: the civil registry issues identity, Digital Government runs the identity broker, the Ministry of Economy accredits signature providers, and a new data-protection agency enforces Law 21.719.

What is open: FEA signature providers are accredited by the Entidad Acreditadora and may be domestic or foreign entities with a presence in Chile. Law 21.719 creates strong demand for consent, data minimisation and biometric protection.

Relevant SAVIS capabilities include TrustCA Remote Signing for advanced and qualified signatures, ID Verification for chip reading and face matching, and Consent Management for Law 21.719-style consent records.
Sources: SRCeI (Res. 234 exenta, 13 May 2026); ChileAtiende; Red GEALC (March 2025); Law 19.799, Decree 181/2002; Law 21.719; Garrigues (October 2026).

title: Australia opens the Government Digital ID System to the private sector from 30 November 2026
sum: Under the Digital ID Act 2024, accredited identity, attribute and exchange providers can join AGDIS — and banks, telcos and rental businesses can rely on it.
body: Australia does not license private “national wallets”. Instead, businesses are accredited as identity service providers (ISP), attribute service providers (ASP) or identity exchanges (IXP) under the Digital ID Act 2024, and then apply to join AGDIS.

For businesses: become an accredited ISP, ASP or IXP and apply to participate in AGDIS — or connect as a relying party. Credential wallets will follow the Commonwealth VC Trust Framework now being built.

SAVIS components that align with the accreditation model include SAM Auth Server (authentication up to AL3 with phishing-resistant FIDO2), SAVIS TrustOnboard (biometric verification with PAD) and Digital ID Wallet (verifier and wallet components).
Sources: Digital ID Act 2024; digitalidsystem.gov.au; Australian Department of Finance (Estimates Brief, February 2026); Mallesons (June 2026); Biometric Update (November 2026).

title: Identity and payments pull each other forward: a verified identity becomes a payment passkey
sum: Digital identity enables instant eKYC; eKYC creates device-bound payment credentials; biometrics replace OTP — and every payment strengthens the identity.
body: Identity and payments used to be separate projects. They are converging into a single loop.

1Digital identity

A verified identity.

2Instant eKYC

Open an account or wallet in minutes.

3Payment credential

A token bound to the device.

4Biometric authentication

A passkey instead of OTP — back to a stronger identity.

Card-network payment passkeys

Payment credentials bound to the device; the customer confirms with the biometric that unlocks the phone; built on FIDO.

National wallets confirming payments

The EUDI Wallet supports SCA for payments; the EWC and NOBID large-scale pilots have tested it.

DPI payment rails

G2P and P2G tied to national identity: benefits reach the right person; fees are collected without cash.

For banks this means the onboarding journey and the payment journey should share the same credential. FIDO2 Passwordless Identity, API Security & Transaction Signing and 3D Secure 2.0 let a passkey created at onboarding approve card, account and wallet payments with dynamic linking.
Sources: industry report on digital identity and payments (January 2025); EUDI ARF 2.8.0; national Digital ID policy of Papua New Guinea (2025).

title: EUDI architecture: issuers, wallet and relying parties on one trust framework
sum: How PID providers, attestation issuers, QTSPs, the EUDI Wallet Unit and relying parties fit together — and the protocols between them.
body: The European Digital Identity framework is a three-sided system — issuers, the wallet held by the user, and relying parties — sitting on a shared trust framework.
Trust framework: Trusted ListsRelying-party registrationWallet provider attestationConformity assessment bodies certify wallets

Two design choices matter most for national implementers. First, where the wallet's keys live: a secure element on the phone, an eSIM, or a remote HSM acting as the WSCD — SAM Appliance supports the remote option. Second, how relying parties are onboarded: registration, access certificates and the verifier stack determine how quickly banks and telcos can actually accept the wallet.
Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183; EUDI ARF; OpenID4VCI / VP; ISO 18013-5; ETSI EN 419 241.

title: Customer consent in banking: new requirements to watch in VietNam
sum: The Personal Data Protection Law 91/2025/QH15 (in force from 1 January 2026) and Decree 356/2025 raise the bar for how banks obtain and manage consent.
body: Decree 13/2023/ND-CP laid the foundation for personal data protection in VietNam. Law 91/2025/QH15 on Personal Data Protection, effective 1 January 2026, and Decree 356/2025/ND-CP now give consent a stronger legal basis.
Consent must be specific to each purpose and cannot be bundled with unrelated purposes. Banks must be able to prove who consented, when and to what — and customers can withdraw consent at any time.

When asking for consent, banks must state the purposes (including credit scoring), retention periods, how to withdraw and how data is deleted. Credentials, card data, transaction history and credit information must be flagged as sensitive data.

Banks must also assess compliance yearly, log all processing activities, apply protection and anonymisation standards, and notify authorities within 72 hours of a leak of sensitive data. SAVIS Consent Management automates collection, storage, verification and withdrawal of consent across digital and physical channels.

title: Protecting personal data when linking with VNeID: what businesses need to do
sum: Decree 320/2026 extends VNeID linking and authentication across 12 sectors. Using VNeID does not mean unlimited use of citizens’ data.
body: Law 91/2025/QH15 on Personal Data Protection took effect on 1 January 2026. Decree 320/2026/ND-CP, effective 28 September 2026, extends requirements to connect and authenticate electronic identity through VNeID, and Decree 330/2026/ND-CP, effective 19 August 2026, sets penalties for cybersecurity and personal data violations.
Transaction accounts in 12 sectors must be linked and authenticated with VNeID, and 206 documents are being integrated on VNeID — businesses may not ask people to present them again.

Businesses should collect only what each process needs; enforce access control, strong authentication and access logging; apply encryption, key management and anomaly monitoring; define responsibilities; keep evidence of who accessed what and when; and manage data through to deletion.

title: Timestamping for securities: proving the moment and integrity of every order
sum: Securities firms must record when orders are received and prove records are unaltered. Trusted timestamps make that evidence hard to dispute.
body: Securities firms must record order receipt times, keep transaction evidence and show that electronic records are reliable. Without traceable records, verifying transactions and resolving disputes is difficult.

The legal basis includes the Law on Electronic Transactions 2023, Decree 23/2025/ND-CP (Articles 24 and 32 on timestamp services), Circular 134/2017/TT-BTC as amended by Circular 73/2020/TT-BTC, and Circular 121/2020/TT-BTC on order records.
A timestamp proves that data existed at a given moment and reveals any later change. With digital signatures, identity verification and system logs, it supports reconciliation and dispute resolution.

title: TrustCA Remote Signing certified for eIDAS 2.0 and NIS2

body: TrustCA, the trust services brand of SAVIS Group, has had its Remote Signing service assessed and certified against eIDAS 2.0 and NIS2 requirements by TAYLLORCOX PCEB (certificate PCEB 26/08/10, covering qualified remote signing, qualified timestamping and eSeal, valid until 9 August 2028).

Remote signing lets people and organisations create legally binding digital signatures from any device, while the private signing keys stay inside a hardware security module and are only used after strong authentication by the signer.

title: Decree 320/2026: three reasons banks should prepare now
sum: New requirements on customer identification and authentication make early preparation the lower-risk path for Vietnamese banks.

title: Harvest now, decrypt later: why post-quantum planning starts today
sum: Data with a long life is already at risk. A practical path to post-quantum cryptography starts with knowing where your cryptography is.
body: Attackers can record encrypted traffic today and keep it until a quantum computer can break the algorithms that protect it. Records that must stay confidential for ten years or more are exposed now.

NIST has published post-quantum standards, including ML-KEM for key establishment and ML-DSA for digital signatures. Migration takes years because cryptography is embedded in applications, devices, certificates and partner connections.

1Inventory

Find every algorithm, key and certificate.

2Rank

By data lifetime and exposure.

3Hybrid

Classical + ML-KEM / ML-DSA where risk is highest.

4Migrate

Roll out with crypto-agility and test in the PQC Lab.

A sound programme starts with a cryptographic inventory, ranks systems by data lifetime and exposure, and introduces hybrid classical and post-quantum protection where risk is highest. The SAVIS Quantum Readiness Program and Quantum PQC Lab follow this approach.

title: eIDAS 2.0 explained: what trust service providers and wallets must change
sum: The European Digital Identity framework extends trust services and introduces digital identity wallets. Here is what changes for providers.
body: eIDAS 2.0 updates the European framework for electronic identification and trust services and introduces the European Digital Identity Wallet.

Trust service providers face updated requirements for security, conformity assessment and new qualified services such as electronic attestations of attributes. Organisations that rely on digital identity will need to accept wallet-based credentials.

Each Member State must offer at least one European Digital Identity Wallet, free for individuals, that holds person identification data and attestations of attributes, supports selective disclosure and lets people sign with a qualified electronic signature for personal use. Public bodies must accept the wallet, and relying parties must register and request only the data they need.
